# What an Agent Credential Lets You Do Next

**A follow-up chapter to “How to Build a Zero-Human Company” — field notes, 2026-11-21**

In the [original guide](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/blob/main/files/how-to-build-zero-human-company-2026-11-20.md), I started with credentials: give the agents their own identity. In the [banking follow-up](/blog/autonomous-company-agent-banking-2026-11-21), I asked who holds the money and who signs. This chapter connects those decisions. A credential is a behavior intervention: it decides what an agent can do next, what stops it, and whose participation it needs to continue.

Our working foundation is an agent mailbox, a team phone number, and a shared credential store. That makes some operations independent of my availability. It does not prove that the accounts belong to agents, that every recovery path is autonomous, or that secrets stay outside model context.

These are dated field notes built from the supplied research, not a fresh product audit. The launches below mostly predate the guide; they are additions to our map, not things that all shipped overnight. Under **What we learned by running it**, I distinguish our operating records from research findings. Reported figures retain their source and scope; **UNVERIFIED** means the supplied research did not establish the claim directly.

## Start with the authority, not the login

### Do this

I now write down these answers before accepting any agent-credential product:

| Question | What I require in the evaluation record |
|---|---|
| Who is the principal? | Identify the person or organization granting authority and carrying responsibility, separately from the agent's identity. |
| Where does the mandate live? | Locate the allowed actions, counterparties, limits, and expiry: in a signed credential, a server policy, or only an instruction to the model. Name the component that enforces them. |
| Does the model ever see the secret? | Trace delivery through the tool process, prompt, tool response, transcript, and logs. A vault alone does not answer this. |
| How does revocation work? | Identify who can stop the agent, what gets invalidated, and what happens to existing sessions and issued credentials. |

For each answer, I distinguish documentation from an observed result. My acceptance procedure is to attempt an allowed action, attempt an action outside the mandate, revoke access, and retry with an already-issued credential. I record the outcomes without recording secrets. This is the procedure I want our stack to pass, not a claim that it already has.

### What we learned by running it

Our [credential inventory](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/blob/main/files/human-credential-inventory-2026-11-20.md) exposes why a successful login is an incomplete test. Apple operations can use agent-accessible infrastructure while the developer account remains legally in my name. The team can receive SMS while the owner and payment source of the telephone account remain unknown. Operational access, legal ownership, and recovery control are separate facts.

The shared store solves a practical handoff problem: work need not stop because the agent that created an account is unavailable. It does not, by itself, restrict each agent's authority or provide a tested kill switch.

### Unverified & caveats

I have not completed the acceptance procedure across our stack. The inventory is evidence of recorded dependencies and migration status, not a universal audit of secret exposure, mandate enforcement, or revocation.

## KYA gives the questions a product category

### Do this

I would start with a written mandate even before buying an identity product. The community [Agent KYA proposal](https://daily-build-portfolio.vercel.app/agent-kya.html), as summarized in the research, offers a useful checklist: `agent_id`, `principal`, `scope`, `vendor_allowlist`, `limits`, `escalation`, and `attestation`.

Those seven fields make authority discussable. I would put allowed actions in `scope`, permitted counterparties in `vendor_allowlist`, and the response to exceeded limits in `escalation`. I would then connect the record to an enforcement point. Writing a signed file does not make a tool obey it.

### What we learned by running it

This part is research, not a deployment. The supplied note describes MetaComp's StableX KYA launch on April 21, 2026 and the open community proposal the following day. It reports Baselayer's Agentic Identity Suite launch on September 22, 2026 alongside a $35 million Series A. The [Baselayer analysis](https://explainx.ai/blog/baselayer-know-your-agent-kya-identity-2026) organizes the problem around the agent, its principal, its mandate, and its counterparty.

The [Zetrix AI and CAICT announcement](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/media-release/zetrix-ai-and-china-academy-information-and-communications-technology-unveil-know-your-agent-kya-service-bring-trust-and-accountability-ai-agents-6527121) dated November 5, 2026 describes verifiable identities linked to businesses or people, explicit delegated permissions, and checks before protected actions. It also describes a cross-border pilot whose results are intended for standards bodies.

The useful change for me is that “an agent has an account” is becoming an insufficient product description. I can ask where its authority comes from and where that authority is checked.

### Unverified & caveats

Baselayer's claimed coverage of 2,300+ financial institutions describes its existing business-identity network, not adoption of its KYA product. The same analysis cites a Stripe claim that 70% of API data-access commands come from agents; that telemetry is **UNVERIFIED** beyond the reporting chain, and I do not use it as adoption evidence.

The open JSON proposal is a community design, not proof of interoperability or an adopted standard. The Zetrix/CAICT announcement supplies a pilot plan, not demonstrated pilot outcomes. I have not deployed these systems.

## Probe an identity before counting it

### Do this

If I publish an agent card, I need its endpoint to answer and describe that agent accurately. When evaluating a registry, I would separate registrations, declared endpoints, responding endpoints, and distinct cards. I would preserve the date and population of each measurement.

A responding card is only the start. I still need to establish who controls it, what mandate it represents, and whether a counterparty checks that mandate before acting.

### What we learned by running it

The research describes ERC-8004 as an identity registry using an ERC-721 token pointing to an agent registration file, with reputation and validation components in the design. It links the [EIP](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8004) and an [overview](https://www.alchemy.com/overviews/erc-8004).

The supplied [census snapshot](https://agenteconomy.to/stats/erc-8004-agents) reports **2,262,198 registrations across 24 chains** as of November 19, 2026, excluding testnets. It also reports that **92.8% of 79,260** registrations during the preceding seven days pointed to agent-card URLs on a single domain. Excluding that domain left **5,669**. The census explicitly distinguishes an identity count from an activity count.

A separate [BAS Doctor run](https://medium.com/@bas_io/how-bas-check-8004-agent-647652f28119), dated November 12, reports this funnel:

| Measurement in that run | Reported count |
|---|---:|
| Registrations considered | 941,487 |
| Registrations declaring an endpoint it contacted | 618,724 |
| Registrations whose endpoints answered | 517,314 |
| Registrations serving their own card after repeated responses were removed | 977 |

The lesson I take is methodological. A registration proves that something was registered. It does not prove that a distinct agent is operating. The probe supplies a stronger observation, but I cannot turn its final count into the number of functioning agents in the whole ecosystem.

### Unverified & caveats

I did not rerun either measurement. The census and BAS Doctor cover different dates and populations; **977 is not the measured remainder of 2,262,198**. A distinct card does not prove activity, safe behavior, or trustworthy ownership. A failed probe does not establish that an agent never operates.

The research's account that the Validation Registry was pulled back for rework and excluded from the official mainnet deployment set remains **UNVERIFIED** against deployment contracts. Our own agent registration and live-card implementation are not demonstrated here.

## Evaluate enterprise identity feature by feature

### Do this

I would use the same evaluation record for Okta, Entra, Auth0, and Vault. Ask the vendor to demonstrate the actual token path and the fate of an existing session after revocation. Check each needed feature's availability separately from the product's launch label.

I would also ask what the billing unit represents. A price quoted per user is insufficient to calculate the cost of a workforce of agents; I need the licensing rule that maps agents, human users, and workloads to charges.

### What we learned by running it

This is a review of the supplied research, not experience operating these products. The [Okta summary](https://docs.openproxyai.com/blog/agent-identity-entra-okta) reports general availability on April 30, 2026, with an agent registry, scoped short-lived tokens, discovery, access certification, and a kill switch. It reports third-party identity-provider support through Cross App Access added on November 13, 2026.

The [Entra/Auth0 comparison](https://www.swytchcode.com/content/entra-agent-id-vs-auth0-for-ai-agents) describes Entra Agent ID blueprints as templates for agent identities. It describes Auth0 Token Vault as brokering third-party OAuth tokens so agents need not hold long-lived secrets. Of five Auth0 announcements in May 2026, it says three were generally available by mid-November; Agent as Principal and FGA Permissions Index were still in early access or developer preview.

[IBM's October 27, 2026 announcement](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-10-27-ibm-introduces-identity-and-control-for-ai-agents,-securing-frontier-intelligence-for-the-enterprise?asPDF=1) describes Vault Agent Identity records containing an owner, lifecycle state, and granted authority, connected to short-lived credentials and revocation controls.

The reported capabilities address real gaps in our shared-store approach. A named agent, scoped authority, and lifecycle control would let me distinguish replaceability from unrestricted access.

### Unverified & caveats

The research's [pricing roundup](https://geekchamp.com/guide-to-choosing-nonhuman-and-ai-agent-identity-tools/) lists Agent 365 at **$15/user/month paid yearly** and Microsoft 365 E7 at **$99/user/month**. Its comparison says dedicated agent-identity pricing was not published as of November 2026. These are reported packaging figures, not executed quotes or proof that each agent incurs a human seat charge.

I have not deployed these products or tested their advertised revocation. Token brokering does not establish that our particular integration keeps tokens out of model context. A directory's accountable owner also does not necessarily imply human approval of each action; operational autonomy and responsibility remain separate questions.

## In payments, locate the signed mandate

### Do this

Before letting an agent buy, I would identify who authorized the purchase, which merchants and limits are covered, and which component checks those conditions. Browsing permission must not silently become purchasing permission.

I would locate the consent record separately from the agent's request signature. Then I would establish how the merchant checks expiry or withdrawal of authority. A valid signature proves something was signed; the surrounding system must decide whether that authority still applies.

### What we learned by running it

The supplied [Cloudflare account](https://blog.cloudflare.com/secure-agentic-commerce/) describes Visa Trusted Agent Protocol and Mastercard Agent Pay building on Web Bot Auth to distinguish approved agents from anonymous bots and carry commerce-related identity signals.

The [payment-identity synthesis](https://eco.com/support/en/articles/15192005-agent-identity-verification-how-ai-agents-authenticate-purchases-in-2026) describes Mastercard's Agentic Token as binding a cardholder, registered agent, and mandate scope, with developer enrollment associated with a KYC'd entity. The [Boston Identity critique](https://insights.bostonidentity.com/glossary/trusted-agent-protocol) argues that Visa TAP's published sample lacks a signed mandate or consent record, contrasting it with Mastercard Verifiable Intent's signed limits.

That distinction sharpens the banking chapter for me. Knowing which agent sent a request and knowing what its principal authorized are different checks. A protocol can address the former while leaving the latter to another part of the payment system.

### Unverified & caveats

The Visa assessment is a third party's reading of published materials, not my test of a production integration. It does not prove that Visa's wider payment system lacks consent controls. The Mastercard description is also reported synthesis, not an implementation we ran.

The research describes Google's AP2 as making user consent cryptographically auditable through verifiable digital credentials. Its primary-spec details remain **UNVERIFIED**. None of these descriptions demonstrates an account without a responsible human or organization, nor a working payment flow in our company.

## Fix our own credential path before buying another identity

### Do this

I would work from our inventory, preserving its distinctions between migratable, partially migratable, non-migratable, and unverified dependencies. For each migration, I would record the registration identity, operational access, recovery path, and legal owner separately.

The next architectural step is to keep secrets in the execution layer. The model should request a scoped action; a tool should retrieve and use the credential, enforce the mandate, and return a result without the secret. I would check failure output and logs as well as the successful response. Where supported, I would prefer workload identity or short-lived leases to broadly shared long-lived credentials.

For the team phone account, I would establish ownership and payment responsibility without publishing their values. I would preserve the trusted number while investigating those dependencies. Renaming an account is not proof that its recovery or funding has become independent.

### What we learned by running it

Our research records **22 inventory items**, not 22 completed migrations. The mailbox, team SMS route, and shared store are working components. Apple operations have a documented VM-based App Store Connect API path and team SMS path, while the developer account's legal name remains mine. The original guide also records an Apple sign-in flow that offered only device push. I cannot honestly translate the available SMS route into “the founder's phone never rings.”

TikTok remains partially migratable because its login source depends on my phone. GitHub repositories remain under my personal account, with some web authentication flows still reaching my phone. The proposed agent account and collaborator arrangement is a migration procedure, not proof it has finished.

The secrets-management research recommends separating model context from credential execution, including in the [DevToCash guide](https://devtocash.com/blog/2026-08-08-secrets-management-devops-ai-agents) and [MetaCTO guide](https://www.metacto.com/blogs/ai-agent-secrets-management-production). That is a stronger boundary than the one our guide established. Sharing a credential store makes agents replaceable; proving that no secret reaches a model requires inspecting the tools that read it.

The research run also records a research CLI failing authentication. That is evidence of a tool-access blocker, not evidence that the external identity products failed. I keep that distinction because diagnosing the wrong layer produces the wrong repair.

### Unverified & caveats

Twilio's account owner and payment method remain **UNVERIFIED** in the supplied inventory. Completion of the new agent-owned X account was **not re-measured**; its status remains in progress / **UNVERIFIED**. This chapter does not perform those migrations or recheck the live accounts.

The [1Password Unified Access description](https://fast.io/resources/best-secret-management-tools-ai-agents/) in the research is a vendor-claim summary, **UNVERIFIED** by a run. I do not cite it as proof that our tools isolate secrets. Nor have I established that our current shared store provides per-agent least privilege or comprehensive revocation.

My next step is therefore concrete: take a dependency from the inventory, identify its principal, locate and enforce its mandate, trace its secret path, and test revocation. That is how I would turn “the agent can log in” into evidence about what it can safely do next.
